title: WIYN 3.5-meter Telescope at sunset, Kitt Peak
camera_perspective: very wide, ground level, mountain-top setting at dusk
visible_characteristics: Wide sunset landscape (2400x1600 saved). The white faceted enclosure sits on a ridge top in the left third of the frame and is small (about 1/20 of the frame width): angular hip roof with a flat cap, lit windows near the base, a tiny white dome beside it. A forested slope falls away to hazy layered valleys on the right; warm orange glow low on the horizon; heavy grey-orange clouds fill the upper half.
scientific_relevance: A 3.5 m class enclosure in its real mountain context: small on the skyline, tree cover, atmospheric perspective in the valleys. Good scale reference for the whole observatory in a wide shot.
production_influence: OBS_004_MOUNTAINS: three ridge layers with haze increasing to the far layer. At true scale the real enclosure is only about 5 percent of frame width here; the storyboard's dome lower-centre framing is a deliberate enlargement, so keep the ridge haze and layering but not the scale. Clouds can be the only sky texture at dusk; at night use the star field only.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: Aerial view of the WIYN 3.5-m Telescope, Kitt Peak, 29 Oct 2012
camera_perspective: high oblique day view, three-quarter from above
visible_characteristics: Telephoto high oblique, day. The metallic enclosure is an octagonal drum with a faceted pyramidal aluminium-grey roof topped by a narrow flat strip (the shutter slot, a ridge-line cut); a band of rectangular louvred vents wraps the drum (one is open, showing blue inside); below it a white polygonal base with a thin blue stripe. A single-storey blue-roofed annex with a car park is attached; a small white hemispherical dome stands at the right edge; granite boulders, junipers, and a flat desert plain fill the background and foreground.
scientific_relevance: Shows a real 3.5 m class enclosure is a rotating faceted drum with vents, an annex and a small neighbouring dome: i.e. not every professional telescope sits under a hemisphere.
production_influence: Roof, drum and base are separate rotation levels: if a rotating shell is ever drawn, the roof+drum rotate relative to the base ring. Boulders and a squat annex are good OBS_007_PROPS (rocks, utility shed).
credit_line: P. Marenfeld/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA and E. Acosta/Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: The New Technology Telescope building at La Silla
camera_perspective: ground level, three-quarter, twilight, portrait
visible_characteristics: Twilight, purple sky. A corrugated-aluminium box building: two tall flat shutter leaves, each about one third of the building width, slid apart to leave a full-height vertical slit; inside you see the telescope truss, a ring and a white mirror structure. Low octagonal drum base with a ring ledge; white annex with doors at the right; a weather-vane mast; cracked concrete apron, stone retaining wall. No hemispherical dome anywhere.
scientific_relevance: A real 3.5 m class alt-az telescope (NTT, 3.58 m) in a box enclosure that rotates with the telescope; ESO caption on the Commons mirror: sliding roof and wall open to the ground, whole building rotates, telescope can point to 10 degrees above the horizon.
production_influence: Gives the second real-world answer to 'what shape is the 3.5 m enclosure'; keep as the alternative silhouette if the owner prefers the film's building to look like APO or WIYN rather than a dome. Shutter leaves must be separate sliding layers.
notes: Filed under observatory (enclosure) even though ESO catalogues it as a telescope picture. Saved width after sips: 1860 px.

title: La Silla telescopes in twilight
camera_perspective: telephoto ground view of a barren summit at dusk
visible_characteristics: Barren brown rock hill at dusk. On the left a white corrugated box building with a lower annex (NTT form); behind and to the right a tall white cylinder topped by a hemispherical dome with a dark vertical slit open at the top (the ESO 3.6 m); between them a small dome; a switchback road, a lone service building and a tiny white dome on a stand at the lower right; purple-blue sky.
scientific_relevance: Shows a hemispherical dome with a slit and a box enclosure side by side on one summit, so both forms are real. The Commons caption calls the large dome 'NTT' while the image content suggests the box is the NTT; I trust the picture over the caption here.
production_influence: Compare silhouettes: dome-on-cylinder reads at a glance from far away, the box does not. Supports choosing the hemispherical dome-on-drum for a 9:16 wide shot.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: ANTU (UT1) and AT1 with the enclosure doors open
camera_perspective: front-on, ground level, golden light
visible_characteristics: Square frame. The huge enclosure front: two flat corrugated shutter leaves slid to either side (outer wall bays), the centre opening shows a dark interior with a big truss and a red round plate on the telescope structure; a fixed beam ledge under the opening; a lower drum wall with sliding panels and round windows; a small white Auxiliary Telescope (a bowl-shaped enclosure with open lattice inside, number '1') in the foreground for scale. Warm low sun from the left, cool shade on the right.
scientific_relevance: Clear picture of bi-parting vertical shutter leaves and the telescope visible through the opening. ESO caption (Commons mirror): 35 m wide, almost 40 m high; AT is 1.8 m.
production_influence: OBS_006_DOME_SLIT: two leaves sliding apart horizontally is the right mechanism for the film; travel equals about half a leaf width each way in this photo. Use warm rim light on one side for the day frame; the night frame uses cool dim light.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: Kueyen opening its enclosure with the telescope tilted
camera_perspective: inside the enclosure, looking up and across from the floor
visible_characteristics: Looking up through steel members into the open VLT enclosure: thick tubular truss legs cross the foreground, a large ring-shaped altitude structure with an actuator ring in the centre, blue steel gantries and a walkway frame overhead, a louvre wall of white horizontal slats at left, pale sky showing through the opened slit at upper left, ducts on the right.
scientific_relevance: ESO caption: the telescope is tilted while the enclosure opens so anything that falls misses the mirror; enclosures open about 5 to 10 minutes before sunset.
production_influence: B01: telescope should sit tilted (not flat) while the slit opens; then tilt up on 'ask' (B03). Structure in the foreground gives the occlusion layer for OBS_003_INTERIOR.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: Fish-eye perspective inside a VLT unit telescope enclosure
camera_perspective: high interior fisheye, full circle with black corners
visible_characteristics: Circular fisheye. Tall polygonal steel walls (blue trusses, silver ducts), the slit open at the top showing white sky; the telescope in the centre (grey box centrepiece, tube truss with a ring at the top); a circular tiled floor with a darker track ring and a red line, orange work-lamp light at lower left, a single person standing on the floor for scale, and a circular railed grating platform around the periphery.
scientific_relevance: Typical interior of a large alt-az observatory: free floor, circular track, ring platform at mid height, ducts, slit overhead. No workstations anywhere near the telescope.
production_influence: OBS_003_INTERIOR: floor ring + railed platform + overhead trusses; the control room is NOT here (it is a separate room), confirming the film can omit workstations. One tiny human figure gives scale; the film should leave the interior unpeopled.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

source_org: International Gemini Observatory / NOIRLab / NSF / AURA
title: Gemini North dome fully open
camera_perspective: front-on, slightly low, daytime, blue sky
visible_characteristics: Front view under deep-blue sky. A dome shell split at the centre by a wide vertical slit; two curved door leaves are retracted to the sides; a flat corrugated wind-screen panel is raised in the lower front of the slit; on both sides large rounded 'shoulders' with white steel lattice vent openings, ladders and handrails run up the sides; a row of small round holes at the very top of the slit; the metal-clad roof of the building fills the foreground bottom.
scientific_relevance: Shows the real wind-screen / baffle: a rectangular panel that rises from the bottom of the slit, plus louvred vent shoulders. Gemini is 8 m, so scale differs, but the parts are the same on smaller domes.
production_influence: OBS_006_DOME_SLIT: add an optional wind-screen panel layer at the slit bottom (separate rectangle, raised while the slit is open). Vent shoulders can be reduced to two rounded bulges plus a few lattice lines for a generic read.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: VLT unit telescope launching a laser (Adaptive Optics Facility first light)
camera_perspective: low ground level, night, three-quarter on the enclosure
visible_characteristics: Night, low camera. A large angular-faced white enclosure with one shutter leaf slid open to the right; an intense orange beam of constant width shoots up and to the right from inside the opening into a star-filled sky; orange glow on the corrugated leaf at upper left and inside a lower dark window; stairs and steel railings in the foreground; other unit-telescope buildings at left and (small) at right; louvred vents along the left; sky deep blue fading to orange at the horizon.
scientific_relevance: Real night view with the slit open: you see the dark opening, the beam leaves from inside, and the building is lit only by the beam and the horizon glow. It is a long exposure of a continuous guide-star laser, not a pulsed ranging beam.
production_influence: OBS_001/OBS_002 night grading: building is a dim cool grey with a warm accent only where the beam spills. Confirms the film's beam must be an explicit symbol; B02 dashed cone is a different, imagined thing.
notes: Beam colour looks orange; I did not read the ESO caption for wavelength or power. Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: View through the open slit of a VLT unit telescope while it fires a laser
camera_perspective: from inside the enclosure, looking up through the slit, portrait
visible_characteristics: Portrait. Looking up from inside through the open slit: a narrow strip of starry sky with Milky Way dust lanes, bounded by dark steel structure on both sides and vent boxes at the top. A wide orange beam crosses diagonally from a cylindrical launch telescope mounted at the side of the telescope (lower centre) toward the upper right, where it ends in a thin tapered head; grey cabinets and a steel truss platform at the bottom.
scientific_relevance: Shows the slit as a tall narrow rectangle of sky and a beam leaving the telescope assembly from a small side launcher; foreground structure partially masks the sky.
production_influence: B22/B24 option: a view from inside the slit with dark structural silhouettes framing a sky strip is a strong occlusion-mask composition (OBS_003_INTERIOR foreground layer).
notes: Different from APOLLO: this launcher is a separate small telescope on the side; APOLLO transmits through the main aperture. Saved width after sips: 1600 px.

title: Interior view of the Mayall 4-m telescope dome
camera_perspective: wide-angle interior from the floor, looking up
visible_characteristics: Wide-angle interior of a big hemispherical dome: ribbed white shell with rows of striped light panels along both sides of the slit; the slit runs up the centre with a grey louvred shutter; the telescope stands in the middle: white truss tube with a ring at the top above a huge blue ring/yoke and blue pier; steel stairs and railed walkways at left and right, red doors, a mesh cage and white concrete walls at floor level.
scientific_relevance: Defines the interior vocabulary: ribbed shell, slit in the middle, fixed platforms and stairs, telescope in the centre. Mayall is an equatorial mount, so only the interior is used, not its mount.
production_influence: OBS_003_INTERIOR background layer: ribbed hemisphere with a central slit; pier platform with a railed stair. Foreground occlusion: stair railings and platform edge in front of the telescope base.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: Telescope silhouetted against the open slit at sunset
camera_perspective: inside the dome, portrait, tube pointing to the slit
visible_characteristics: Portrait, dark interior. The telescope's tube truss is in black silhouette (white truss pipes catching a little light, a ring and dark secondary hub at the upper end) pointing toward the open slit; the slit frames a glowing orange sunset with the Sun at the horizon and blue sky above; a shutter ladder and gantry stand at the right edge of the slit; fluorescent tube lights are at the upper left and upper right; a white mirror-cell box at the lower left.
scientific_relevance: Shows what the telescope looks like against the sky through the slit: a near-black cut-out with thin truss lines, the ring and the secondary housing at the top.
production_influence: B03/B24 silhouette test: the telescope reads mainly as a ring + thin diagonal struts + a dark secondary hub; the mount disappears in darkness. Occlusion: the slit edge crosses in front of the tube top.
notes: Saved width after sips: 1787 px.

title: Corner reflector ray diagram (isometric cube corner, two rays)
camera_perspective: oblique 3-D view of a cube corner cut away to three faces; rays enter from the upper right
visible_characteristics: Pale lavender-blue cube corner with a darker left face, a medium floor face and a light back face, each with a thicker lighter rim. Two ray paths with arrowheads: a black ray pair on top and a red ray pair below. Each ray enters from the right, bounces off the faces in turn (visible kinks on the left wall/floor) and leaves toward the right again; the outgoing line sits beside, not on top of, the incoming line and runs the opposite way (arrowheads reversed). No text, no axes. (Viewed through a 1000 px PNG render I made from the SVG with qlmanage, saved next to the original.)
scientific_relevance: Three mutually perpendicular reflecting faces send a ray back antiparallel to its entry direction, laterally displaced (C06).
production_influence: B19-B21: draw the ray as one continuous polyline with a small lateral offset between entry and exit lines; keep arrowheads on every segment. Keep the third-face inset (B20) because a 2-D cross-section can show only two faces.
notes: SVG is vector; the _render.png beside it is my qlmanage render, not an original.

title: Comparison of retroreflectors: corner (1) and spherical cat's-eye (2)
camera_perspective: 2-D side cross-sections, stacked vertically, incoming light from the left
visible_characteristics: Two stacked panels labelled 1 and 2 in large black numerals on white, each with a grey back block. Panel 1: two thick blue mirror faces meeting in a right angle opening to the left; a solid orange ray enters horizontally at the top, hits the upper face, drops vertically, hits the lower face and leaves horizontally leftwards with an arrowhead, i.e. exactly reversed and offset downward. Red dashed and green dotted off-axis rays also bounce twice and come back toward the upper left. Panel 2: a pale cyan sphere with a blue back arc; the orange ray refracts in, reflects once off the back and exits; red and green rays do similar but miss the exact reverse direction. Colour-coded line styles (solid / dashed / dotted) separate ray families. (Viewed via qlmanage PNG render.)
scientific_relevance: Shows the 2-D slice of a corner cube: two reflections, exit antiparallel and offset; contrasts it with a cat's-eye retroreflector.
production_influence: B20/B21: use this panel-1 geometry for the cutaway rays (two bounces in the slice). Use several ray styles at different heights so 'any entry angle' is visible. Note it is NOT a flat-mirror comparison (see gaps).

title: Gold first-surface corner-cube retroreflector (photo)
camera_perspective: 3/4 high angle looking into a black cylindrical mount, white background
visible_characteristics: A black anodised cylindrical housing with a square flange (two bolt holes at the bottom corners). Inside the round opening, a dark amber-gold interior with three thin bright seam lines meeting near the lower centre, and an irregular many-sided aperture edge at upper left. Glassy dark-gold look, speckle dust on the faces, no sharp reflections of the environment. Hollow, first-surface mirror type (per the file description), not a solid glass prism.
scientific_relevance: Real corner cubes show the three-face seams meeting at the apex; faces are mirror-coated.
production_influence: B19: the macro push into one cube should end on the apex with three seams meeting, not on a plain glass disc. Solid fused-silica Apollo cubes are glass (C05); this hollow gold one is a different construction, so use it for the seam geometry only.

title: Corner-cube ray path, rotating 3-D animation
camera_perspective: animated, camera orbits a transparent cube while a red marker travels along a ray
visible_characteristics: Frames sampled (every 1 s, 12 tiles, contact sheet in research/video_analysis/gif_corner_cube_wikimedia/). Black background, grey cube drawn as three visible faces with white edges, later turned semi-transparent. A thick yellow polyline ray enters from the top, kinks at three faces and leaves upward again; a red ball rides the head of the ray and leaves a yellow trail. Later frames add a second parallel entering ray and rotate the view to a side-on angle where the two rays are visibly parallel and the faces form a corner. 151 frames, 10.6 s.
scientific_relevance: Animated proof that entry and exit rays are parallel and that three reflections occur.
production_influence: B20: leading dot + persistent trail is the clearest way to show path order; rotate the view once to prove parallelism, or show two entering rays together (see sampled frames).
notes: Animation: reviewed as FRAME_SAMPLED, not watched in real time.

title: APOLLO return-photon scatter plot, 8 December 2005
camera_perspective: 2-D data plot: x = time (minutes), y = time into the detector gate (ns)
visible_characteristics: White background, small black dots. Title '8 December 2005'. X axis 'time (minutes)' 0 to about 12.5; Y axis 'time into gate (nanoseconds)' 0 to 120. Roughly 2,500 dots scattered uniformly over the whole area (background), plus a dense, perfectly horizontal heavy line of dots at about 46 ns running the whole width with two or three short gaps (around 4 min, 9.5 min). The signal is a flat band at constant arrival time; the background is evenly scattered.
scientific_relevance: Real APOLLO data: returns appear as a stable band at fixed delay inside a noisy gate (C08).
production_influence: B26-B27/B29b: build the 'signal emerges' scene as dots on a time-into-gate axis, one column per pulse, background uniform, signal at a constant offset. The horizontal band is the real look; the histogram is the projection of it. Counts stay labelled illustrative.
credit_line: APOLLO Collaboration, CC BY 3.0 (via Wikimedia Commons)
notes: Low resolution (491x360). Axis ticks readable, dot count only estimated by eye.

title: Gaussian beam envelope: waist, Rayleigh range and divergence angle
camera_perspective: side view, beam axis horizontal (z), radius vertical (w)
visible_characteristics: White background. A blue hyperbola-like pair of curves pinching to a narrow waist at the centre, with straight dark-red dashed asymptotes crossing at the waist and opening outward to the left and right. Dimension arrows and symbols: w0 at the left, z0 (green) between centre and a vertical marker, sqrt(2) w0 at the right, small theta and large Theta as angle arcs in dark red. Axes: blue vertical 'w', green dash-dot horizontal 'z'.
scientific_relevance: Beam divergence geometry: the beam is hyperbolic near the waist and cone-like far away.
production_influence: B25: at lunar distance we are in the far field, so draw straight cone edges from an apex; do not draw a waist. Use the asymptote style (dashed edge lines) if a footprint inset needs an angle marker.

title: Gaussian beam waist and divergence (labelled)
camera_perspective: side view, beam axis horizontal
visible_characteristics: Red hyperbola pair pinching at the centre, light-blue dashed asymptotes, black dimension arrows: w0 (waist radius), sqrt(2) w0, b (confocal parameter) across the top, zR (Rayleigh range) below, w(z) at the right, Theta as a curved double arrow between the asymptotes, grey axis z with arrow. Italic mathematical labels. The lower half of my render is blank because the SVG canvas is taller than the drawing.
scientific_relevance: Same concept as REF-OPT-006 with a cleaner dimension-line style.
production_influence: Dimension-line style (thin black double arrows with end ticks) is a template for B09/B33 brackets as well.

title: Simulated star image through turbulence, telescope aperture D = 2 r0
camera_perspective: negative (dark-on-white) image of a point source
visible_characteristics: Square white field with a thin black border. A single compact dark core slightly left of centre, softly blurred, with a faint pale ring-like halo and two or three faint dark lobes (one upper left, one right) around it: a nearly clean diffraction pattern, slightly distorted.
scientific_relevance: Small aperture relative to turbulence scale: image wanders but stays one blob.
production_influence: B29: the mild case is a footprint that moves and distorts as one body.
credit_line: Wikimedia Commons, public domain (per file page)

title: Simulated star image through turbulence, aperture D = 20 r0
camera_perspective: negative image of a point source
visible_characteristics: Same framing as REF-OPT-008 but the single core is gone: a cloud of many tiny dark speckles filling a roughly round patch about a quarter of the frame wide, no bright centre, very low contrast.
scientific_relevance: Large aperture: speckle pattern; the light is split into many wandering spots.
production_influence: B29: for the 'magnified' disturbance use a speckle breakup of the footprint, not a smooth sine wobble.
credit_line: Wikimedia Commons, public domain (per file page)

title: Plane waves entering a turbulent layer become perturbed wavefronts
camera_perspective: side view, light travelling downward
visible_characteristics: White canvas, black serif labels. At the top 'Plane waves from distant point source' above three straight horizontal grey lines. A pale cyan band with wavy upper and lower edges labelled 'Turbulent layer in atmosphere'. Below the band about ten stacked grey lines that are now wiggly, with local steps and bumps, labelled 'Perturbed wavefronts'. The lower part of my render is blank (canvas taller than drawing).
scientific_relevance: Turbulence delays parts of the wavefront by different amounts.
production_influence: B29: show straight parallel lines becoming wiggly after the air band; that is also the visual reason for 'arrival time a little uncertain'.
credit_line: Gringer / Wikimedia Commons, public domain (per file page)

title: Seeing: lunar crater field shimmering (animated)
camera_perspective: telescopic close-up of lunar surface, 8 frames
visible_characteristics: Tiny 150x150 grey animation (8 frames at 5 fps, 1.6 s, three tiles viewed). A lunar crater field with a large dark shadow at right; between frames craters shift a few pixels and blur differently, edges wobble but the scene stays recognisable.
scientific_relevance: Visual character of seeing: small random frame-to-frame displacements and blur.
production_influence: B29: wobble amplitude is a few percent of object size, random per frame, not periodic.
credit_line: Philipp Salzgeber / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0 AT
notes: Very small; only a technique reference.

title: Goddard Laser Ranging Facility beams aimed toward the Moon (Observe the Moon Night, 18 Sep 2010)
camera_perspective: ground-level, portrait; wide-angle looking up at a bright Moon
visible_characteristics: Portrait night photo (stored 1713x2400). Deep blue-navy sky with faint stars. A very bright Moon with starburst flare at upper left. Two thin, perfectly straight green beams: one climbs almost vertically from a small white dome at lower left; the other runs diagonally from a telescope on a platform at lower right up to the Moon. The beams are narrow, constant in width, slightly brighter near the source and fading higher up; the diagonal one reaches the bright Moon disc at the top. Telescope pad has railings and a person; red-lit foreground. No visible pulses, the beams look continuous.
scientific_relevance: Real ranging lasers (532 nm green) are visible from the side only by scattering off air; the Moon is a bright disc well off the beam end.
production_influence: B01-B04: the ground-view beam should be a thin straight green line with soft edges that fades with height; do not extend it visually past the atmosphere. Colour conflict with 'outbound warm' flagged in notes.
notes: This is the Goddard facility aimed at LRO, not at an Apollo array (page caption). Downscaled from 2227x3120 to 1713x2400 with sips.

title: Double beams shoot into the night sky (inOMN 2010)
camera_perspective: ground-level, wide landscape, dome in lower centre
visible_characteristics: Dusk-blue sky with scattered stars. A white observatory dome with open slit at lower centre. From the slit a wide green fan-shaped beam rises to upper left, clearly broader at the top than at the dome (perspective plus spread) with brighter green edges inside the dome slit. A second, very thin straight green line runs from the lower right to the top right. Beams look soft-edged and continuous.
scientific_relevance: Two beams of very different apparent width at once: a narrow beam and a wide near-field beam.
production_influence: B25/B20 inset: a real beam is thin; the apparent fan is perspective and should not be read as the km-wide lunar footprint.
notes: Downscaled from 3000x1996 to 2400x1597.

title: Two beams flash across a starry sky toward the Moon (inOMN 2010)
camera_perspective: ground-level, wide landscape, long exposure
visible_characteristics: Dark blue sky with faint short star trails. A bright Moon at upper right with halo. A thin green line runs from the top-left corner to the Moon; another thin line rises from a dome silhouette behind trees at lower centre to the Moon. Lines are straight, uniform and faint, brightest where thick. Tree line and building edge at the bottom right.
scientific_relevance: Shows the faint scattered line look: thin, almost uniform, easily lost against bright sky.
production_influence: B02-B04: keep beam opacity low (about a quarter of the Moon's brightness); it should read as a faint line, matching 'faint scattered line' target (g).
notes: Downscaled from 3000x1996 to 2400x1597.

title: Photograph of a laser guide star beam
camera_perspective: dark sky, vertical-ish beam rising from the bottom edge
visible_characteristics: Near-black star field with many fine white/blue stars. A single thin, sharply defined golden-yellow line rises from the bottom edge, leaning slightly right, and ends abruptly in a tiny bright dot about halfway up the frame, with nothing beyond. Thinner and tidier than the GSFC beams.
scientific_relevance: Good model for how a beam looks when it leaves the air: it simply stops where the air is too thin to scatter.
production_influence: B04/B05: the beam line stops at the top of the atmosphere before the match cut to space; a pulse symbol then takes over. Yellow here is a sodium (589 nm) guide-star laser per the file title, not a ranging laser.
credit_line: Gunter Schuricht / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
notes: Downscaled from 3008x3008 to 2400x2400. The sodium-laser identification comes from the file title, not from the image.

title: The Basics of Lunar Ranging (page image cartoon.gif)
camera_perspective: schematic of ranging geometry (Earth turbulence, return beam spreading)
scientific_relevance: Page text (read via fetch summary): ~1 arcsec outgoing beam, ~1.8 km at the Moon; reflector returns ~8 arcsec, ~15 km footprint; one in ~30 million photons hit the reflector; 2.34-2.71 s round trip range quoted.

title: Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR) deployed on the surface (AS11-40-5952)
camera_perspective: three-quarter view from the front, a few metres away (distance estimated by eye), array face tilted up toward the upper left
visible_characteristics: The deployed Apollo 11 array seen from the front-left and slightly above. The face is a flat rectangular panel made of a dark, glossy grid of cube faces; it reads as near-black with small bright glints, set in a silver-grey aluminium box. The panel is tilted so its face points up and to the left (toward the sky); the box edge facing the camera shows a thin lip and rivets. Below it is a white-bright base plate that rests on the soil, with angled struts and a tall bail-handle arch (a thin rectangular loop) at the right. Two thin rods lie on the ground at the left (gnomon/stowed legs). The surrounding soil is dark grey, rough, with chevron bootprints in the foreground. In the distance, upper left, the LM leg; upper right, the PSEP mast on its copper-coloured base. The base is much brighter than the panel face because it is sunlit white metal while the face is dark glass.
scientific_relevance: Primary photograph of the Apollo 11 LRRR in its deployed configuration: a tilted flat array with a support frame, not a dish.
production_influence: RETRO_001/RETRO_004: draw a silver-grey aluminium box with a white-bright base plate and bail handle; the cube faces read as a dark glossy grid (not round glassy bubbles). Tilt the face upward toward the camera's upper left.
notes: Saved copy is the Wikimedia public-domain NASA scan (2349x2373). The ILRS 904x913 version of the same frame has sha256 080ad882b01b38fc611d3aaa5207f8e0cc3ba7f657a50c446914ffed35d71fbf and is not saved separately. PSR fig 7-7 is the same frame. title: Corner reflector: ray path (3-D)

Faces are shaded in three tones.

title: Casio digital watch in stopwatch mode reading 0'01"41

title: Omega Speedmaster Professional chronograph, dial and bezel

Central chronograph seconds hand is a long thin white hand with a pointed tip; a second central hand and the hour/minute hands are cream with luminous centres, plus a small luminous dot at 12. title: ESO New Technology Telescope, looking up along the tube

camera_perspective: three-quarter from the floor beside the bearing, portrait

Thick grey/white tubular truss legs rise from a large blue circular altitude bearing and a large rectangular grey box (centrepiece); two workers in hard hats at the lower left give scale (the bearing is about 3 to 4 people tall); grey cabinets with red/orange indicator lamps are attached to the box; a blue ladder; dark ceiling girders in blue.
scientific_relevance: ESO caption: Nasmyth adaptor-rotator in the foreground, instruments on the adjacent Nasmyth platform. 8.2 m class, so larger than APO's 3.5 m, but the bearing + centrepiece + truss layout is the same alt-az logic.
production_influence: TEL_002_MOUNT: bearing is a big disc, not a small pin; centrepiece box carries the tube; cabinets on the box side are optional detail but would be 'invented dials' so keep them as plain rectangles.
notes: Saved width after sips: 2256 px.

title: VLT Unit Telescope 2 in its enclosure during integration
camera_perspective: three-quarter, low, portrait
visible_characteristics: A grey polygonal top ring joined by four large tubes to a long rectangular grey centrepiece box that has round holes in its side; a blue circular altitude bearing / Nasmyth adaptor sits at the left; the lower part shows a grated platform; dark blue ceiling girders and silver ducts fill the top.
scientific_relevance: ESO caption: mirror cell was about to be mounted; first light expected Mar 1999. Shows the centrepiece box as the frame that links the tube, bearing and mirror cell.
production_influence: TEL_001_HOUSING: tube = ring + four legs + box; the box is the big visual mass, the ring is small relative to it. Separate layers: ring+legs (rotate with tilt) and box (tilts with it).
notes: Saved width after sips: 2243 px.

title: VLT UT4 mirror cell on a transporter
camera_perspective: side view in daylight, outdoors
visible_characteristics: Daylight. A bright yellow lorry hauls a very wide grey-white mirror cell on an orange transporter: a shallow bowl of triangulated white truss under a flat top ring covered with small dark actuator hardware; at upper left a white hemispherical Auxiliary Telescope dome with a rounded opening on a concrete base with a railing; brown rock cut and a gravel road.
scientific_relevance: ESO caption: UT4 (Yepun) mirror cell being moved for recoating. Shows the primary sits in an open lattice cell with many actuators; and that a small dome with an open slit is just a hemisphere with a rounded cut.
production_influence: TEL_004_PRIMARY_CUTAWAY: simplified bowl under the mirror; do not draw actuator detail. Do not use the lorry. Small AT dome is another dome-with-slit shape cue.
notes: Not a telescope-in-use image; supports the cell structure only. Saved width after sips: 2400 px.

title: Installation of the M2 unit on VLT UT1 (10 Mar 1998)
camera_perspective: ground level on the enclosure floor, portrait

title: New primary mirror cell for the WIYN 3.5-m telescope (1995)
camera_perspective: high oblique from above, whole cell
visible_characteristics: From above: a light-blue octagonal plate carrying a black circular ring (the mirror seat), a grid of white cylindrical support posts and several brass actuators; a round central hole (cyan walls, orange/red hardware visible below); eight grey blower fans around the perimeter; eleven people stand behind it for scale (the cell is about five or six people wide); the light-blue telescope structure frames the background.
scientific_relevance: A 3.5 m class mirror cell without the mirror: the primary rests on a field of supports, and a big central hole lets light pass behind the mirror to a Nasmyth/Cassegrain port.
production_influence: TEL_004_PRIMARY_CUTAWAY: concave mirror with a central hole, resting on a cell; the return light path goes through the hole in one common Cassegrain layout (APOLLO's actually leaves the side via folding mirrors M3/M4/M5, per Murphy et al.).
notes: Photo dated 1995 per NOIRLab caption. Saved width after sips: 2000 px.

title: Installing the WIYN 3.5-m primary mirror on its cell (1995)
camera_perspective: eye level, close, side-on to the mirror edge
visible_characteristics: The mirror hangs from slings and a spreader bar, wrapped at its rim in a bright yellow protective band; its pale top surface with a round central bore is just visible; below is the blue octagonal cell with white support posts, brass actuators and grey fans; three people look on, one pointing; orange hardware at the base.
scientific_relevance: Shows the mirror's thickness relative to its diameter (a thin disc, rim height about 1/20 of its diameter in this view) and the central bore.
production_influence: TEL_004: draw the primary as a thin concave disc with a central hole, not as a thick dish. Cutaway thickness ratio about 1:15 to 1:20.
notes: Thickness ratio is my estimate from the photo. Saved width after sips: 1998 px.

title: Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope interior
camera_perspective: low three-quarter looking up the tube, portrait
visible_characteristics: Portrait. The white truss tube with a top ring is tilted up; a dark secondary housing with a jagged baffle skirt hangs below the ring at the top; a grey mirror-cell box with vents sits at the base; a huge blue circular ring (the horseshoe/yoke face) fills the frame; an orange support carriage with a railing is at the bottom; ribbed dome shell and slit shutter behind.
scientific_relevance: Mayall is equatorial (not alt-az), but the tube, ring, secondary baffle and mirror-cell box are what any Cassegrain reflector looks like.
production_influence: TEL_001_HOUSING: baffle skirt on the secondary and a vented cell box are good identifying details; the mount from this photo must NOT be copied (equatorial).
notes: Equatorial mount: use only for tube and cell details. Saved width after sips: 1578 px.
